name_en: Sri Lankan Mutton Curry (Elu Mas Curry)

ingredients.name: Mutton (bone-in, shoulder or leg)
ingredients.notes: cut into 3-4cm pieces; bone-in gives far better flavour than boneless

ingredients.name: Vinegar
ingredients.notes: apple cider or white; tenderises the meat and adds slight sourness

ingredients.name: Salt
ingredients.notes: for the marinade plus more to taste

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.notes: more may be needed for longer braising

ingredients.name: Thick coconut milk
ingredients.notes: added once the mutton is tender

steps.instruction: Rinse the mutton in water with a little turmeric, then drain well. Marinate with the roasted curry powder, chilli powder, turmeric, black pepper, vinegar, and salt for at least 30 minutes, ideally overnight in the fridge.
Heat the coconut oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and fennel seeds. Let them sizzle for 30 seconds.
Add the sliced onions and cook until softened and light golden, about 5-7 minutes.
Add the garlic, ginger, curry leaves, pandan leaf, and lemongrass. Cook for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the chopped tomatoes and cook until they break down into a thick paste, about 4-5 minutes.
Add the marinated mutton. Stir well and fry for 5-7 minutes until the meat is browned on the outside.

Add water, enough to just cover the meat. Bring to a boil, then reduce to low, cover, and simmer for 60-70 minutes, checking occasionally and adding a little more water if the pot dries out, until the mutton is completely tender.
Pour in the thick coconut milk. Stir gently and simmer uncovered for 15-20 minutes on low heat until the gravy is rich and thick. Taste and adjust salt. Serve with rice, string hoppers, or roti.

source_site: theflavorbender.com, cross-checked against islandsmile.org, rasapadhama.wordpress.com, yogurtsoda.com, ceylonsupermart.com, and topsrilankanrecipe.com
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 6+ independent sources; strong agreement on overnight marinade, bone-in meat, and adding coconut milk only once the meat is tender
notes: Mutton (goat meat) curry uses the same base technique as beef curry (sl_035) but mutton has its own stronger, gamier flavour profile and requires thorough washing (sometimes in turmeric water) before cooking to reduce any strong smell. Bone-in pieces are strongly preferred across all sources -- the marrow enriches the gravy considerably. A Jaffna-style variant (kari) uses a heavier hand of roasted curry powder and is typically drier and spicier, with less or no coconut milk; this entry reflects the more widely cooked coconut-milk version common across all communities. Like beef curry, this tastes significantly better the next day.
